name: Deep Saffron
lede: Deep Saffron is a strong, warm orange named for the dye and spice taken from crocus stigmas, and our archive's earliest match for it predates the color's own written record by nearly four centuries, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin.

sections.title: A spice, by way of a flag
sections.body: Saffron comes from the dried stigmas of the saffron crocus, among the most labor-intensive dyes and spices ever traded, and Wikipedia's citation for this exact shade is the flag of India, whose top stripe is called saffron [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[ochraceous-orange]], [[yellow-orange-color-wheel]], [[dark-orange]] and [[mikado-orange]], at 2.8, 3, 3.4 and 4 ΔE [1]. 68 among the Yellows, matched to the anthers of the saffron crocus and the tail coverts of the golden pheasant [2], a step short of [[yellow]] itself. 8, 3, 3.4 and 4 ΔE [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Deep Saffron appears in just 0.13 percent of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, 31 of them as photographed, rarer than 53 percent of the named colors we track [4]. Inside a painting it almost always plays an accent, in 98 percent of its 40 clearest appearances, never the body of a shadow or a light [4]. It peaks in the 1500s, in 6 of 2,231 paintings, at 1.5 times its own museums' baseline [4].

The earliest match is a 1445 painting by Michele Giambono, well before any of our Western sources first record the word saffron as an English color name; Werner's 1821 guide is the oldest system we hold that names this family at all [2][4]. It belongs to the [[orange]] family, sitting a step brighter than plain [[saffron-yellow]] [3].
